title: Compute Has Shape: Self-Morphing the Internal Computation of Frozen LLMs
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:Compute Has Shape: Self-Morphing the Internal Computation of Frozen LLMs
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Test-time scaling improves large language models through additional computation, but how to adapt the topology of internal computation to individual inputs remains underexplored. Existing approaches largely fix recurrent or parallel architectures during training, or reconfigure frozen models along a single structural axis. We introduce SelfMorph, which makes computational shape an input-dependent inference-time decision. It unifies the original forward path (BASE), serial reuse of a layer span (REPEAT), and local branching and merging of perturbed hidden states (BRANCH) in a unified space parameterized by type, location, and intensity. Since they offer complementary benefits rather than uniform dominance, we use a lightweight selector that reads the backbone's depth-wise hidden state trajectory on the prompt to choose a morphology before response generation. We train the selector by distilling utility-based distribution from offline morphing that jointly account for task performance and computational cost. Evaluated on three LLMs spanning 4B-27B, SelfMorph achieves a 8.06% mean relative improvement on five in-distribution benchmarks and 4.45% on four unseen benchmarks. It achieves the strongest performance in 24 of 27 settings. These findings identify input-adaptive computational topology as a complementary axis of test-time scaling beyond generating more tokens. Our code is available at this https URL.

report.summary: SelfMorph lets frozen LLMs choose per-prompt internal computation shapes—base, repeated layers, or branched paths—improving test-time scaling beyond simply generating more tokens.
report.background: Test-time scaling has become a major way to improve large language models without retraining: models can generate longer chains of thought, sample multiple answers, or spend more compute during inference. But most methods focus on adding tokens or samples, not on changing how computation flows through the network. Existing recurrent or parallel architectures are usually fixed during training, and prior work on frozen-model reconfiguration tends to adjust only one structural axis. SelfMorph explores a different lever: the topology of internal computation. It asks whether a model can decide, per prompt, whether to run the original forward path, reuse a layer span serially, or branch and merge hidden states locally. This matters because different inputs may benefit from different compute patterns, and frozen models are widely deployed.
key_points: SelfMorph treats computation topology as a per-input inference-time choice. Instead of always running the same layer stack, it can use the original forward path, repeat a layer span serially, or branch and merge perturbed hidden states locally.

A lightweight selector reads the backbone's depth-wise hidden-state trajectory on the prompt, then chooses a morphology before response generation. It is trained by distilling a utility-based distribution from offline morphing runs that jointly account for task performance and computational cost.

The method is evaluated on three LLMs ranging from 4B to 27B parameters. It reports an 8.06% mean relative improvement on five in-distribution benchmarks and 4.45% on four unseen benchmarks, achieving the strongest performance in 24 of 27 settings.

The paper frames input-adaptive computational topology as a complementary axis of test-time scaling. Rather than only generating more tokens or sampling more candidates, models can spend compute in different structural patterns matched to the prompt.

The approach keeps the backbone frozen and adds a selection layer, making it attractive for adapting deployed models without full retraining. The code is promised via the arXiv page, though independent reproduction and serving-stack integration remain to be tested.
report.impact: For the AI industry, SelfMorph points to a broader view of inference scaling: quality gains may come from reshaping computation, not just lengthening outputs. That could influence how serving systems schedule work, since different prompts may trigger different layer-reuse or branching patterns. For developers, the appeal is adapting frozen models with a lightweight selector and forward-path modifications rather than retraining. It also suggests new benchmarking questions: how to measure compute savings alongside accuracy, and how well selectors generalize to unseen tasks. For regular users, the practical payoff would be better answers at similar or lower cost, especially if serving stacks can exploit the chosen morphologies efficiently. The main caveats are selector overhead, integration complexity, and whether gains hold outside the evaluated benchmarks.
report.tools: Watch the paper's promised code release on arXiv. For hands-on experimentation, Hugging Face Transformers forward hooks and custom generation loops can prototype layer repetition, branching, and early exit; vLLM or SGLang matter for serving-level integration. Related open-source lines to follow include Mixture-of-Depths, LayerSkip, and adaptive-depth or recurrent-depth implementations.
